claims.text: The initial material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy in nanoscale thin-film form.
The as-deposited film has an inherently random microstructure and grain-boundary distribution.
Decreasing nanoribbon width increases the edge-to-volume ratio relative to a continuous film.
Lateral confinement and the increased edge-to-volume ratio cause magnetic-domain fragmentation.
Narrower nanoribbons exhibit enhanced grain-boundary or interfacial magnetic effects.
Edge defects and confinement increase domain-wall pinning.
Edge defects and confinement induce additional spin disorder.
Increased domain-wall pinning and spin disorder hinder coherent domain rotation.
The high surface area of the nanoribbons limits rapid thermal equilibration through constrained heat transfer.
Nanoscale confinement will reduce the peak magnetic entropy change relative to a continuous film.
Narrower nanoribbons will have greater magnetic hysteresis than the continuous-film baseline.
Narrower nanoribbons will display a broader M(H) response than the continuous-film baseline.
The proposed behavior applies during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles below 1 T.
The proposed behavior applies at temperatures near the alloy's magnetic transition.
Heat-transfer rates limit the usable magnetic-cooling cycle frequency in the stated regime.
Patterning films into a controlled series of decreasing ribbon widths while holding thickness and composition constant provides the proposed intervention.
Peak magnetic entropy change and M(H) hysteresis are relevant observables for comparing magnetocaloric behavior.
Width-independent entropy changes and hysteresis profiles statistically equivalent to those of the continuous film would falsify the confinement hypothesis.
